lines.text: On the thirtieth of June 2012, the world added one second to the clock.
Within minutes, Reddit went down. An airline in Australia couldn't check in its passengers. Servers across the internet froze.
All because of a second that, on most clocks, isn't even allowed to exist.
That second exists because of something most people never hear: right now, nobody on Earth knows exactly what time it is.
Not your phone. Not the satellites overhead. The official time for this moment will be worked out weeks from now, in an office outside Paris.
This is the story of who decides what time it is — and why we stopped trusting the Earth to do it.
For most of history, time came from the Sun. When it was highest in the sky, it was noon.
lines.section: I. Every town had its own noon (0:45–2:10)

lines.text: Which meant every town had its own noon. In Bristol, it came about ten minutes after London's.
lines.section: I. Every town had its own noon (0:45–2:10)

lines.text: The clock on Bristol's Corn Exchange still has two minute hands. One for Bristol. One for London.
lines.section: I. Every town had its own noon (0:45–2:10)

lines.text: Then came the railways. A timetable with a different time at every station was a recipe for collisions. In 1880, Britain made Greenwich time the law.
lines.section: I. Every town had its own noon (0:45–2:10)

lines.text: And a second was still just a slice of a day: one eighty-six-thousand-four-hundredth of a turn of the Earth.
lines.section: I. Every town had its own noon (0:45–2:10)

lines.text: There was only one problem. The Earth is a terrible clock.
lines.section: I. Every town had its own noon (0:45–2:10)

lines.text: The tides drag on it like a brake. Earthquakes, melting ice and the churning core nudge it faster, then slower. No two days are exactly the same length.
lines.section: I. Every town had its own noon (0:45–2:10)

lines.text: So in the 1950s, scientists stopped looking up at the sky — and looked inside an atom instead.
lines.section: II. The atom that never gets tired (2:10–3:30)

lines.text: A caesium atom absorbs microwaves at one exact frequency. Every caesium atom in the universe has the same one. It never wears out. It never slows down.
lines.section: II. The atom that never gets tired (2:10–3:30)

lines.text: In 1955, near London, Louis Essen built the first clock that counted those microwaves. And it showed something awkward almost immediately.
lines.section: II. The atom that never gets tired (2:10–3:30)

lines.text: The atom was keeping perfect time. It was the planet that was wobbling.
lines.section: II. The atom that never gets tired (2:10–3:30)

lines.text: Astronomers had kept the world's time for centuries. They did not give it up easily. It took twelve years.
lines.section: II. The atom that never gets tired (2:10–3:30)

lines.text: In 1967, the second was redefined: nine billion, one hundred and ninety-two million, six hundred and thirty-one thousand, seven hundred and seventy vibrations of caesium. Exactly.
lines.section: II. The atom that never gets tired (2:10–3:30)

lines.text: That solved one problem and created another. Atomic time is perfect. Earth time is not. And people still want noon to happen when the Sun is high.
lines.section: III. The second that breaks computers (3:30–5:00)

lines.text: So since 1972, whenever the planet falls almost a second behind the atoms, the world adds one. 23:59:59. Then 23:59:60. Then midnight.
lines.section: III. The second that breaks computers (3:30–5:00)

lines.text: It has happened twenty-seven times. And the one in 2012 is the one that took down Reddit.
lines.section: III. The second that breaks computers (3:30–5:00)

lines.text: Software assumes a minute has sixty seconds. Give it sixty-one, and some of it simply stops.
lines.section: III. The second that breaks computers (3:30–5:00)

lines.text: Google stopped playing along. Now it smears the extra second across a whole day, running its clocks very slightly slow until the second has quietly disappeared.
lines.section: III. The second that breaks computers (3:30–5:00)

lines.text: In 2022, the world gave up. The leap second will be abolished by 2035, and atomic time and the Sun will be allowed to drift apart.
lines.section: III. The second that breaks computers (3:30–5:00)

lines.text: But there's a twist. Lately, the Earth has been spinning faster. For the first time in history, the next leap second might have to be taken away.
lines.section: III. The second that breaks computers (3:30–5:00)

lines.text: So who actually decides what time it is? Not one clock. Even atomic clocks drift, each in its own way.
lines.section: IV. Four hundred clocks vote (5:00–6:15)

lines.text: Instead, more than four hundred atomic clocks in about eighty laboratories send their readings to the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, just outside Paris.
lines.section: IV. Four hundred clocks vote (5:00–6:15)

lines.text: There they are compared and averaged. The steadiest clocks get the biggest vote. The result is Coordinated Universal Time — the time the whole world runs on.
lines.section: IV. Four hundred clocks vote (5:00–6:15)

lines.text: And here is the strange part. The answer is published once a month — for the month that has already gone.
lines.section: IV. Four hundred clocks vote (5:00–6:15)

lines.text: Official time only ever exists in the past. Every clock you own is showing a prediction of what that answer will turn out to be. Usually right to within a few billionths of a second.
lines.section: IV. Four hundred clocks vote (5:00–6:15)

lines.text: Your phone gets its time from satellites, twenty thousand kilometres up, each carrying atomic clocks.
lines.section: V. Clocks in the sky (6:15–7:15)

lines.text: Up there, time runs differently. Weaker gravity makes their clocks run fast. Their speed makes them run slow. Add it up, and each one gains thirty-eight millionths of a second every day.
lines.section: V. Clocks in the sky (6:15–7:15)

lines.text: Leave that uncorrected, and your map would be wrong by around ten kilometres — by tomorrow.
lines.section: V. Clocks in the sky (6:15–7:15)

lines.text: So the satellite clocks are built to tick slightly slow on the ground. In orbit, Einstein makes them right.
lines.section: V. Clocks in the sky (6:15–7:15)

lines.text: The newest clocks use light instead of microwaves. Lift one by a single centimetre, and it measurably ticks faster.
lines.section: VI. The last digit (7:15–8:00)

lines.text: Time isn't even the same from floor to floor. Walk upstairs, and your head ages faster than your feet — we made a whole video about that.
lines.section: VI. The last digit (7:15–8:00)

lines.text: So what time is it, right now? The honest answer is: we'll know next month. Until then, four hundred clocks are voting.
lines.section: VI. The last digit (7:15–8:00)

lines.text: The last digit of time is always a little bit in the future.
lines.section: VI. The last digit (7:15–8:00)
